content: The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on the management of chronic pain in children were developed through a structured and evidence-based process. The process involved multiple stakeholders, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), external technical experts, and WHO technical officers. External experts and members of the Evidence Review Group (ERG) participated in discussions but were not involved in the final consensus or voting process. The guideline methodologist played a critical role in guiding the GDG and co-chairs in interpreting evidence, understanding GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) certainty-of-evidence assessments, and translating evidence into actionable recommendations. WHO recommendations were formulated through a consensus-driven process, where all GDG members either agreed with or accepted the recommendations, including their wording, direction, and strength (strong or conditional). Minor disagreements on wording or rationale did not preclude consensus. If consensus could not be reached, an anonymized online vote was conducted, requiring an 80% approval threshold for any recommendation. Confidentiality was a key component of the guideline development process. At the start of the guideline development process, WHO technical officers conducted a scoping review to identify existing systematic reviews addressing key questions. Databases such as PROSPERO, the Cochrane Library, Epistemonikos, and the Campbell Collaboration were searched. However, none of the identified reviews were deemed comprehensive or up-to-date enough to serve as the basis for the guidelines. Consequently, WHO commissioned systematic reviews to evaluate the effectiveness, harms, and acceptability of physical, psychological, and pharmacological therapies for managing chronic pain in children. These reviews also included qualitative evidence synthesis to capture the experiences and sociocultural acceptability of interventions from the perspectives of patients, caregivers, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders. The GRADE system was used to assess the certainty of quantitative evidence for each critical and important outcome. For qualitative evidence, confidence was based on factors such as methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. These assessments were presented to the GDG in evidence profiles to inform discussions and recommendations. The GDG used the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework to formulate recommendations during a virtual meeting held in September 2020. This framework considered factors such as the priority of the problem, the balance of benefits and harms, certainty of evidence, values placed on outcomes, equity, resource implications, and feasibility. Recommendations were categorized as either strong or conditional, based on the GDG’s confidence in the balance of desirable versus undesirable effects. Strong recommendations indicated high confidence that the benefits outweighed the harms, while conditional recommendations reflected less certainty and emphasized the need for shared decision-making with patients. In addition to intervention-specific recommendations, the guidelines included guiding principles based on human rights and ethical considerations, as well as best practice statements derived from clinical and public health experience. These principles and statements did not require systematic reviews of evidence, as they were considered universally applicable and non-controversial. Following the GDG meeting, the draft guidelines were reviewed and approved by WHO technical officers, the GDG, and external peer reviewers. Peer review focused on technical feedback, clarity, and implementation considerations but did not alter the agreed-upon recommendations. The guidelines underwent WHO’s internal quality assurance process and were approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee and senior leadership. WHO committed to monitoring research developments in the management of chronic pain in children, particularly in areas with low or very low certainty of evidence. Unless new evidence necessitates an earlier review, the guidelines will be systematically reviewed and updated five years after publication. Stakeholder input will be sought to address emerging interventions and considerations. The guideline development process involved a diverse group of contributors, including internal WHO staff, external experts, systematic review teams, and observers. Selection criteria emphasized expertise, geographic diversity, and gender balance.
